questions.text: An office building plan is 25m (E-W) × 18m (N-S) in Cebu (Type IV climate). Identify the primary design problem for cross-ventilation and propose a solution.

options.text: East-west exposure is insufficient; rotate plan 45° diagonal for optimal solar orientation, which may not be feasible due to site constraints
Tropical ventilation requires sealed spaces to prevent external heat penetration; cross-ventilation is unnecessary, which contradicts passive cooling strategies
Window area is too small; increase facade openings to 50% to maximize air velocity, which may affect structural integrity
Plan width (25m) exceeds the 15m effective cross-ventilation depth; interior zones lack fresh air. Solution: interior courtyard (6m×6m) creating two 9.5m zones on each side

rationale.a: Solar orientation optimization is secondary to ventilation effectiveness in tropical design.
rationale.b: This contradicts tropical passive design philosophy; sealed spaces are counter to vernacular proven practice.
rationale.c: Asymmetric sizing (small inlets, large outlets) is optimal, not uniform 50% openings.
rationale.correct: The 15m rule: 'Buildings wider than 15–18 meters struggle to ventilate interior zones; interior courtyards or atria become necessary.' The solution (atrium splitting the plan) is explicitly provided as the tested answer.
rationale.takeaway: The 15m rule: 'Buildings wider than 15–18 meters struggle to ventilate interior zones; interior courtyards or atria become necessary.' The solution (atrium splitting the plan) is explicitly provided as the tested answer.

questions.text: A hospital in Quezon City (Type IV) must maintain comfortable spaces for patients. How should architects integrate light shelf design with daylighting and cooling requirements?

options.text: Light shelves should use reflective finishes on both shelf and ceiling to maximize brightness and reduce cooling load equally, ensuring optimal energy efficiency
Light shelves are unnecessary if electric lighting is provided; focus on mechanical cooling instead, as it offers more consistent results
Light shelves work best in arid climates; Type IV high humidity reduces their effectiveness significantly, making them less viable

Light shelves reduce window-area heat gain by 30–40% while achieving 2–3× greater interior illumination; specular (mirror-like) aluminum + diffuse ceiling is optimal for redirecting high-angle noon sun deep into building

rationale.a: Mirror ceiling creates secondary glare; diffuse ceilings are required for health-appropriate non-glare illumination.
rationale.b: Light shelves reduce mechanical cooling demand by 35–40%; they are highly relevant to tropical hospital design.
rationale.c: Humidity does not reduce light shelf effectiveness; they work equally well in Type IV's perpetual moisture.
rationale.correct: Light shelves reduce window-area heat gain by 30–40% while achieving 2–3× greater interior illumination... specular aluminum shelves outperform matte finishes; however, diffuse ceilings (not mirrors) must receive the redirected light.' This is the precise protocol for tropical daylighting integration.
rationale.takeaway: specular aluminum shelves outperform matte finishes; however, diffuse ceilings (not mirrors) must receive the redirected light.' This is the precise protocol for tropical daylighting integration.

questions.text: Calculate the required overhang depth for an east wall in Manila (8am, summer) with 4m sill height, given solar altitude 10°. Then determine why this depth alone is insufficient without additional shading.

options.text: Overhang depth = 4m × tan(10°) ≈ 0.7m (practical). This blocks noon sun but misses early 6–8am exposure when altitude is <10°, necessitating additional shading solutions
Overhang depth = 4m / sin(10°) ≈ 23m. Vertical fins are unnecessary if overhang is deep enough, although this depth is impractical for most urban settings
Overhang depth = 4m / tan(10°) ≈ 22.7m (impractical). Insufficient without vertical fins blocking low-angle morning sun
East walls require minimal shading because morning sun is cooler than afternoon sun, which is a common misconception in tropical climates

rationale.a: Calculation is reversed (should be height / tan, not height × tan); also misidentifies altitude at 8am.
rationale.b: A 23m overhang is structurally and aesthetically implausible; vertical fins are mandatory for practical design.
rationale.d: Morning sun may be cooler but creates glare and psychological discomfort; early heat gain must be controlled.
rationale.correct: Using depth = height / tan(altitude): 4m / tan(10°) = 22.7m—clearly impractical. Early morning (6–8am) has even shallower angles (<10°), requiring additional vertical fins or brise-soleil to block oblique-angle low sun. 2–3m overhangs PLUS vertical fins for east facades.
rationale.takeaway: 2–3m overhangs PLUS vertical fins for east facades.

questions.text: Explain the relationship between orientation strategy and ventilation strategy in tropical architecture. Why can a poorly shaded N-S elongated building outperform a poorly ventilated E-W elongated building?

options.text: Ventilation effectiveness (cooling load reduction 60–80%) exceeds shade benefit (30–50%); poor ventilation cannot be compensated by good orientation. Conversely, excellent ventilation partially overcomes poor orientation through continuous air movement

North-south orientation is universally superior regardless of ventilation quality, because the reduced solar gain on the longer north and south facades eliminates the need for cross-ventilation, making shading alone sufficient for thermal comfort in all tropical climates

Orientation matters equally to ventilation; neither can compensate for deficiency in the other, as solar geometry and wind patterns contribute identical proportions to thermal comfort, meaning a failure in either parameter results in proportionally equal overheating

East-west orientation is optimal; ventilation is secondary to shading geometry because elongating along the east-west axis maximizes prevailing wind exposure, while narrow north-south facades naturally limit solar gain without requiring additional shading devices

rationale.b: Orientation does not overcome poor ventilation; occupants will remain thermally uncomfortable.
rationale.c: This overstates orientation importance; tropics prioritize ventilation > shading > orientation.
rationale.d: This reverses the hierarchy; ventilation is primary, orientation secondary in tropical design.
rationale.correct: The ALE often tests whether students recognize that shading and ventilation trump orientation.' Cross-ventilation effectiveness (6–12 ACH with synergistic stack effect) provides dramatically greater cooling than orientation alone. A poorly ventilated building cannot escape its thermal load; a poorly shaded but well-ventilated building can dissipate heat through air movement despite unfavorable aspect ratio.
rationale.takeaway: A poorly ventilated building cannot escape its thermal load; a poorly shaded but well-ventilated building can dissipate heat through air movement despite unfavorable aspect ratio.

questions.text: What is the 'Venturi skirt' design mentioned as a passive cooling innovation for overhangs in tropical architecture?

options.text: A horizontal fin array that blocks oblique solar angles while maintaining vertical light penetration, enhancing daylighting
A sealed plenum chamber beneath overhangs that buffers thermal radiation and reduces heat transfer to interior spaces
A reflective paint coating on soffit surfaces to reduce re-radiation of trapped heat, improving thermal comfort
A 30–45 degree louver beneath overhangs that accelerates wind flow and increases cooling by creating local pressure drop

rationale.a: This describes horizontal shading; not the dynamic wind-acceleration principle of Venturi geometry.
rationale.b: This describes a thermal buffer; not the Venturi acceleration mechanism.
rationale.c: Soffit reflectance is a separate strategy; not the Venturi skirt.
rationale.correct: : 'The "Venturi skirt" design—a 30–45 degree louver beneath overhangs—accelerates wind flow and increases cooling.' This uses fluid acceleration principle (constriction creates pressure drop) to enhance passive cooling beneath shaded eaves.
rationale.takeaway: : 'The "Venturi skirt" design—a 30–45 degree louver beneath overhangs—accelerates wind flow and increases cooling.' This uses fluid acceleration principle (constriction creates pressure drop) to enhance passive cooling beneath shaded eaves.

questions.text: Why would a developer's proposal for thick concrete walls in an Eastern Visayas project (Type II, no dry season, nighttime 24°C) represent a design error?

options.text: Concrete absorbs moisture, causing structural failure in perpetually damp climates, especially when not properly treated with moisture barriers

Type II nighttime temperatures (24°C) prevent thermal mass discharge; concrete absorbs daytime heat and re-radiates at night, degrading comfort. Alternative: lightweight block + insulation + continuous ventilation
Concrete requires high embodied carbon; BERDE would penalize the choice, leading to lower sustainability ratings and potential regulatory issues
Thick walls block cross-ventilation, reducing air circulation by 40–50%, which can lead to increased reliance on mechanical ventilation systems

rationale.a: While moisture durability matters, the fundamental issue is thermal performance failure.
rationale.c: Embodied carbon is a secondary BERDE consideration; thermal performance is primary.
rationale.d: Wall thickness alone does not block ventilation if windows remain properly sized; the core problem is thermal ineffectiveness.
rationale.correct: The thermal mass error in Type II is explicitly addressed: 'Type II climate prevents nighttime thermal discharge (insufficient ΔT between wall [25°C] and ambient [24°C]). Concrete mass will trap daytime heat and re-radiate at night, degrading comfort.' The proposed alternative (lightweight block + ventilation) is the correct design response.
rationale.takeaway: Concrete mass will trap daytime heat and re-radiate at night, degrading comfort.' The proposed alternative (lightweight block + ventilation) is the correct design response.

questions.text: In tropical climates, what is the primary cooling mechanism that differs fundamentally from temperate-zone passive design?

options.text: Thermal mass storage of daytime heat for release during cool nights, which is less effective in tropical climates due to minimal temperature variation
Ventilation (cross-ventilation, stack effect, wind acceleration) is the primary mechanism; thermal mass is ineffective due to suppressed diurnal range
Orientation to maximize south-facing winter solar gain for heating, which is not applicable in tropical regions
Reflective surfaces to mirror solar radiation back to atmosphere, reducing heat absorption in buildings

rationale.a: This is arid-climate doctrine; it fails in tropics where nighttime temps are too high.
rationale.c: Tropical orientation prioritizes shade and ventilation, not winter heating gain (unnecessary in tropics).
rationale.d: Reflectance helps but is secondary to active air movement strategies.
rationale.correct: The hierarchy: 'In tropical climates, ventilation is the primary cooling mechanism—not shade alone, not mass, not orientation.' Nighttime temps (22–25°C) prevent thermal mass from radiating stored daytime heat.
rationale.takeaway: The hierarchy: 'In tropical climates, ventilation is the primary cooling mechanism—not shade alone, not mass, not orientation.' Nighttime temps (22–25°C) prevent thermal mass from radiating stored daytime heat.

questions.text: A bay kubo-inspired residential design incorporates open floor plan, large windows (30–40% wall area), and slat flooring. Which passive cooling mechanisms does this vernacular exemplar employ simultaneously?

options.text: Cross-ventilation only; other mechanisms are secondary, which limits the design's effectiveness
Cross-ventilation (wind-driven), stack effect (buoyancy via open floor and roof vents), and evaporative cooling (permeable sawali/flooring)
Thermal mass buffering combined with solar orientation optimization, which is not typical for this design
Active mechanical ventilation with natural light backup, which contradicts the passive design principles

rationale.a: The bahay kubo achieves 8–10 ACH through synergized mechanisms, not single-strategy reliance.
rationale.c: Thermal mass and solar orientation are secondary in vernacular tropical design.
rationale.d: The bahay kubo is passive; mechanical systems are absent by definition.
rationale.correct: A well-designed tropical building operates all three simultaneously: Cross-ventilation, Stack effect, Venturi effect.' The bahay kubo exemplar demonstrates: 'Cross-ventilation (large windows all sides), Stack effect (open floor + roof vents), Evaporative cooling (sawali walls, permeable flooring).' This triple integration is the tested standard.
rationale.takeaway: A well-designed tropical building operates all three simultaneously: Cross-ventilation, Stack effect, Venturi effect.' The bahay kubo exemplar demonstrates: 'Cross-ventilation (large windows all sides), Stack effect (open floor + roof vents), Evaporative cooling (sawali walls, permeable flooring).' This triple integration is the tested standard.

questions.text: Compare lightweight construction (timber, metal stud, bamboo) versus heavyweight construction (concrete, masonry) in tropical climates. Which statement correctly reflects research findings?

options.text: Heavyweight is better only in Type III/IV zones; weight is neutral in Type I/II climates, where other factors dominate
Heavyweight construction is universally superior; thermal mass reduces peak cooling by 6–8°C, providing consistent comfort
Both perform identically; construction weight is irrelevant to tropical thermal performance, as other variables are more significant
Lightweight construction is 2–3°C cooler during occupied hours (8am–6pm) vs. heavyweight; nighttime cooling techniques are 35.9% more effective in lightweight structures

rationale.a: Lightweight is optimal in all tropical Coronas types; the difference is marginal in Type III/IV only because diurnal range is slightly larger, not because heavyweight becomes advantageous.
rationale.b: This is arid-climate logic; it explicitly fails in tropical suppressed diurnal range.
rationale.c: Weight dramatically affects thermal response; lightweight structures have faster adaptation to ventilation cooling.
rationale.correct: Research: 'Lightweight timber or metal framing responds quickly to cooled air from night ventilation or early-morning stack effect; interior temperature drops 2–3°C faster than heavyweight buildings. Nighttime cooling techniques are 35.9% more effective in lightweight structures.' This is the evidence-based consensus for tropical design.
rationale.takeaway: Nighttime cooling techniques are 35.9% more effective in lightweight structures.' This is the evidence-based consensus for tropical design.

questions.text: Contrast the roof insulation strategy in tropical climates versus temperate climates. What different purpose does insulation serve in each?

options.text: Both climates use insulation to minimize heat transfer; the mechanism is identical, though the specific materials and thicknesses may vary
Tropics require thicker insulation (150mm+) because humidity reduces effectiveness; Temperate can use thinner 50mm, as the primary concern is temperature differential

Tropics: Insulation prevents heat ingress (cooling load reduction); Temperate: Insulation prevents heat loss (heating load reduction). 50–75mm tropical insulation is adequate; 100–150mm is over-specification
Insulation effectiveness is independent of climate; thickness is determined by building code uniformly, though practical applications may differ

rationale.a: Mechanism differs; the directional heat flow and purpose are opposite.
rationale.b: Humidity does not require thicker tropical insulation; 50–75mm adequately blocks inbound solar heat.
rationale.d: Climate directly determines optimal insulation thickness; uniform codes ignore regional thermodynamic reality.
rationale.correct: In tropics, insulation prevents heat *ingress*, not heat loss (unlike cold climates). 50–75mm is sufficient... BERDE penalizes excess insulation as embodied carbon waste.' This climate-specific logic is fundamental to tropical passive design.
rationale.takeaway: BERDE penalizes excess insulation as embodied carbon waste.' This climate-specific logic is fundamental to tropical passive design.

questions.text: A heritage bahay kubo must be upgraded with typhoon-resistant sliding doors and insect screens while preserving passive ventilation. Identify three design interventions that maintain cooling effectiveness.

options.text: Specify aluminum-frame sliding doors with ventilation louvers (15% aperture when closed), perforated metal insect screens (50% open area), and maintain elevated slat floor to preserve under-structure ventilation
Seal all openings with tight-fitting doors/screens; install mechanical cooling systems to compensate for ventilation loss
Replace bamboo screens with solid walls; compensate with larger roof vents to enhance airflow
Accept ventilation loss; upgrade insulation instead to improve thermal comfort

rationale.b: Sealing defeats the entire bahay kubo design philosophy and ventilation effectiveness.
rationale.c: Solid walls eliminate cross-ventilation; roof vents alone cannot compensate (stack effect requires inlet/outlet balance).
rationale.d: Insulting ventilation with mechanical systems is the opposite of sustainable vernacular preservation.
rationale.correct: Tested answer explicitly includes: '(a) Specify aluminum-frame sliding doors with ventilation louvers; when closed, louvers maintain 15% aperture area for stack flow. (b) Replace traditional fabric insect screens with perforated metal (aluminum 50% open area)... (c) Maintain elevated slat floor by raising door sills 300–500mm, preserving under-structure ventilation.' All three interventions are required for modernization without ventilation loss.
rationale.takeaway: (c) Maintain elevated slat floor by raising door sills 300–500mm, preserving under-structure ventilation.' All three interventions are required for modernization without ventilation loss.

questions.text: A tropical courtyard design includes water features (fountains, pools) intended to cool occupants via evaporative effect. Under what climate conditions is this strategy effective, and where does it fail?

options.text: Effective in Type I dry season (RH 40–50%); limited in Type II perpetual moisture (RH 75–85%) where evaporative potential is reduced 60–70%. Type II requires drainage/prevention of mosquito breeding instead
Water features provide 1–2°C temperature reduction in all tropical climates through evaporation, assuming optimal placement and maintenance
Water features are ineffective in tropics; humidity is too high for any evaporative cooling, making alternative cooling methods necessary
Water features always increase humidity, worsening thermal comfort regardless of climate type, unless combined with mechanical ventilation

rationale.b: While 1–2°C is the magnitude, effectiveness varies dramatically with humidity levels.
rationale.c: Type I dry season provides clear evaporative cooling benefit; not all tropics are equally humid.
rationale.d: Water features increase humidity locally but provide net cooling through evaporation; this is biophilic benefit despite humidity rise.
rationale.correct: Courtyard water features increase relative humidity locally and reduce air temperature by 1–2°C through evaporation.' Performance is climate-dependent: Type I dry season (RH 40–50%) maximizes evaporative cooling. Type II perpetual dampness (RH 75–85%) reduces evaporative potential by 60–70%. Courtyards can trap stale air if poorly oriented; drainage must prevent mosquito breeding in wet climates.'
rationale.takeaway: Courtyards can trap stale air if poorly oriented; drainage must prevent mosquito breeding in wet climates.'.
